web_evidence.title: Room: A Novel — Excerpt
web_evidence.note: A sustained excerpt reproduced with Little, Brown's permission shows Jack continuously narrating his actions, memories, perceptions, and thoughts as I.

web_evidence.title: Confinement and the Transnational in Emma Donoghue's Room
web_evidence.note: This peer-reviewed structural analysis explicitly identifies Jack as a first-person narrator and says both the Room and Outside portions are filtered through his viewpoint.

web_evidence.title: Room by Emma Donoghue
web_evidence.note: The publisher describes the novel as told in five-year-old Jack's voice and from his perspective.

web_evidence.title: An Interview with Emma Donoghue
web_evidence.note: Donoghue states that Jack tells the story, calls him the child narrator, and says he tells the whole story across the novel's two halves.

web_evidence.title: Review of Room by Emma Donoghue
web_evidence.note: The Kenyon Review identifies Jack as the novel's narrator and analyzes the book's sustained narration in his child voice before and after the escape.

person_note: The Goodreads material repeatedly exposes Jack as a participating I-narrator in scene narration, reflection, recollection, and speech beats. The authorized excerpt independently demonstrates the same first-person voice, while a peer-reviewed whole-book analysis explicitly identifies Jack as the first-person narrator across both the Room and Outside portions. Publisher copy, Donoghue's interview, and the Kenyon Review corroborate that Jack tells the whole story. Gnomic sayings and unframed direct speech were treated as non-base material, and the isolated dialogue-address 'you' is not second-person narration. No credible evidence indicates another sustained base person; the main limitation is that the authorized prose excerpt covers only a local portion, resolved by the whole-book structural sources.
